extracted.intended_audience: theologians, clergy, and learned Christian readers (early modern audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria from Hobbes' discussion for deciding what counts as worship, image, idolatry, scandal, and how to interpret scriptural passages about spirits and possession. Useful for theological or historical analysis of religious practices and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is Worship
rubrics_metrics.description: "To Pray to, to Swear by, to Obey, to bee Diligent, and Officious in Serving: in summe, all words and actions that betoken Fear to Offend, or Desire to Please, is Worship, whether those words and actions be sincere, or feigned."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worship is measured by inward value (honour) but is signified by outward words and actions. Examples: praying, swearing, obedience, diligent service. Anti-pattern: treating only external gestures as worship without attending to inward intention; nevertheless outward signs are ordinarily called worship (cultus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Divine and Civil Worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Divine worship is the honor due to God alone; civil worship is honour shown to men in authority (e.g., kings). "To fall prostrate before a King... is but Civill Worship: And he that but putteth off his hat in the Church... worshippeth with Divine Worship."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish by the object and by the inward intention: civil acts (removing hat, prostration) are not idolatry if the actor intends only human respect. The scriptural Greek terms douleia (bond-service) and latreia (service) are used interchangeably; one must not rely purely on verbal labels to distinguish Divine from Civil worship. Anti-pattern: inferring divine worship solely from words or gestures without considering belief about the object's nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Image (strict and broad senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: An IMAGE (strictly) is the resemblance of some thing visible (reflections, apparitions, dreams). In a larger sense, an image is any representation of one thing by another (an earthly sovereign the image of God). "It is also evident, that there can be no Image of a thing Infinite... therefore there can bee no Image of God."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish phantasmal images (ideas/phantasmes) from material objects made to resemble them. Examples: reflections, poetic monsters, carved statues. Principle: invisible or infinite things cannot properly have images; material representations of fancied beings are at best images of the maker's phantasm. Use this to judge claims that an object 'represents' God or spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: When worship of an image becomes Idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: Idolatry occurs when one voluntarily performs external acts that signify honour either to the matter of the image (wood, stone, metal), to the phantasm the matter represents, or to both together; or when one believes such things hear prayers or see devotions. "To worship an Image... is voluntarily to doe those externall acts, which are signes of honoring either the matter of the Image... or the Phantasme..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key tests: (1) Is the worship directed to the matter or to a fancied divine presence? (2) Is the worship meant as devotion proper to God (e.g., asking for things only God can do)? (3) Was the image set up for religious use without divine or legitimate pastoral authority? Anti-patterns: honoring an image as a mnemonic or monument (civil honour) is not idolatry if not believed to be a divine recipient of prayers.

rubrics_metrics.name: External compulsion and non-idolatrous acts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person performs acts of worship under compulsion (terror of death or punishment) without inward honour, those acts are not idolatry. "If hee that doth it, should suppose the Soule of the Prince to be in the Stool, or should present a Petition to the Stool, it were Divine Worship, and Idolatry. ... But if he be compell'd... it is not Idolatry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge by inward assent: outward performance under threat does not evidence internal worship. Caveat: if the actor is a pastor or influential person, even outwardly-compelled acts may scandalize others and thus be sinful. Example: an unlearned man coerced by an idolatrous sovereign who detests the idol inwardly is excused morally, though endurance of martyrdom would be superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scandalous Worship (seeming worship) as distinct sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Scandalous Worship is outward, seeming worship done perhaps under fear and without inner belief; it may be a sin if done by persons whose example misleads others. "Scandalous Worship... may sometimes bee joined with an inward, and hearty detestation... and is neverthelesse a sin... because following their ways, they cannot but stumble."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the actor's social role: if a pastor or respected teacher externally honors an idol (even out of fear) and does not make his unwillingness evident, he scandalizes others and commits sin. Anti-pattern: excusing pastors' public compliance as mere prudence without considering the effect on congregational conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized divine images vs private invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Images appointed or commanded by God (e.g., the Cherubins over the Ark, the Brazen Serpent) were set up to worship God before them and are not examples to imitate for private religious inventions. "They were not set up for the people, or any man to worship; but that they should worship God himselfe before them..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate images instituted by divine command or legitimate authority from images made by private men for religious use. The latter violate the second commandment. Historical example: Hezekiah broke the Brazen Serpent because the people idolatrously worshipped it. Use origin and authorization as key criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting visions and making images from fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing or painting after a fancy is not inherently sinful; but making the picture a representation of God (or holding it to be such) is idolatry. "I say not, that to draw a Picture after a fancy, is a Sin; but when it is drawn, to hold it for a Representation of God, is against the second Commandement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible uses: monuments of friends, memorials, civil honors. Forbidden use: attributing divine power to painted images or using them as objects of devotion. Anti-pattern: assuming all depictions of holy persons constitute worship rather than memorial or instructive art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting scriptural references to spirits and possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural phrases should be read with attention to their language and context: e.g., "led by the Spirit" vs "in the Spirit" may indicate a vision rather than bodily possession; 'Satan entered into him' can signify hostile intention or wicked cogitations rather than literal demonic entrance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use textual comparison (different gospel wordings), natural explanations (disease, frenzy), and reasoned interpretation rather than assuming literal corporeal spirits. Example: Jesus 'being led' into the wilderness is better read as a vision than as physical possession; the 'entering' of Satan into Judas can denote his wicked purpose. Anti-pattern: insisting on corporeal, incorporeal, or demonic explanations without weighing linguistic and contextual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: On extraordinary gifts and their historical limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary gifts (casting out devils, speaking with new tongues, signs listed in Mark 16:17) were likely given "for no longer a time, than men trusted wholly to Christ" and were withdrawn when the Church sought worldly authority and riches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect present-day universality of apostolic miraculous signs; evaluate claims of miraculous gifts against historical context and the institutional condition of the church. Anti-pattern: using expectation of unchanged miraculous gifts to judge contemporary ministers' legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and pastoral duty to remove images that cause idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian sovereigns and pastors ought to remove images which their subjects have been accustomed to worship, to prevent idolatry: "Christian Soveraigns ought to break down the Images which their Subjects have been accustomed to worship; that there be no more occasion of such Idolatry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy guidance: authorities should suppress practices and objects that foster idolatry among the ignorant. Rationale: ignorant people may truly believe images have divine power, and leaving them in place perpetuates idolatry. Anti-pattern: tolerating public images on grounds of tradition without regard to their effect on popular belief.
